translations.text: March 30. The Life of our venerable father John, abbot of the holy mountain of Sinai, who was surnamed Scholasticus.
As for which earthly city it was, a wondrous one, so to speak, that bore and raised this good man before he became a monk, I have no need to speak of it.
But which it is now that has received this marvelous man and feeds him with foodless food, that I do not fail to know; rather, I know it very well. For he is now in that city as well,

Of that city Paul cries out with a loud voice, saying: "whose citizenship is in heaven." There he was fed with immaterial food and gazed on the beauty of the invisible God, of whom one never has enough.
Gazing only with the rational mind, and marveling, he received the worthy rewards of his labors, and crowns.
He has been numbered with those, and abides forever with those, whose feet stand in uprightness. And how, indeed, there
he ran together with the immaterial and took his stand, [being] material [?], I will tell plainly. When the blessed one was sixteen years old in age, but a thousand in understanding,
skill, when he presented himself like a pure, freely offered sacrifice to the great High Priest,
He brought his body to Mount Sinai and his soul, I think, to the heavenly mountain, so that from that very place [?] toward the great but invisible [?].
he resolved to acquire right conduct and progress. And living there, he took up great humility and cut off from himself all his own will.
And he bowed his neck to humility.
And so he willingly put passion to death, as though he had a soul without reason and without a will of its own, and as though his natural being had been completely changed.
And this is more marvelous: that in this great wisdom of his, by a simple life and by humility, he drove away the pride that comes from wisdom. Then, in the nineteenth year,

having sent his teacher ahead to the most high King, as a kind of envoy and advocate, he went out to a place of silence, carrying in his hand, as a weapon for his own strengthening, the prayers of the abbot.
He took up residence in a place five stadia away from the monastery. The name of that place was Tholas. He spent forty years living there,
without growing weary and with burning love,
and with divine
fire continually blazing within him.
And who is able to declare in words his virtues and the labors that he performed while dwelling there?

Nevertheless, let me relate at least a little of the beginnings of this blessed man's good resolve. He ate of everything, but very little, for the sake of the commandment; he was not made proud by this, but acted so that he might always keep humility.
And he kept himself well away from every kind of unguent [?]. At all hours,
thinking on death, he roused his soul to greater labors.
By obedience he cut off the enmity of the tormentor as with a sword.
By seclusion and silence he killed glory, which is worthless as a spider's web. And how shall I relate the crowns that he wove for himself in our presence by the flowing of his tears,
whose secret work remains even until now in the cave that stood a little distance from his hut?
There he would always sit weeping with tears, crying out and shouting loudly, as though someone had pierced his eyes with a weapon.

He took only enough sleep to keep from losing his mind through sleeplessness. Above all, before sleeping he would offer prayers and read books, for this alone brought him relief from despondency. His course was unceasing prayer,

And his love toward God was without measure. Night and day he gazed on God in the purity of his life, as in a mirror, and could not have enough. A certain Moses, one of the monks who were there, wished to imitate his life and begged the abbot to have John take him under his care,
so that he might be his disciple. The abbot pressed John with entreaties, and John took him under his care.

And Moses stayed with him. One day Father John ordered Moses to go to a certain place, dig a ditch to divert water, and bring it for watering the vegetables. When he reached the appointed place, he did what had been ordered without sloth.
When the heat came at midday, Moses lay down under a great rock, fell asleep, and rested.
But the Lord, not wishing harm to his servants, acted beforehand, as is his custom. For while the great-minded father was in his cell, making prayer to God,
He dozed off and fell into a short sleep, and he saw someone with the splendor of a bishop rousing him, reproaching him for sleeping, and saying: "John, how can you sleep so carelessly?"
while Moses is in great danger?” He immediately sprang up and prayed for his disciple.
Then, when he returned in the evening, he asked him, “Did anything bad happen to you?”
He replied, “A large rock nearly crushed me while I was resting beneath it at midday.”

if he had not suddenly called out to me, so that I woke and jumped away. But the truly humble father, without revealing anything he had seen, secretly praised the good God. He was also an example and a healer of invisible wounds, as once with a certain man named Isaac.
Gripped hard by the weight of the flesh-loving demon and fallen into despair, he ran to this great-minded father, and with tears and wailing he confessed the harm of his warfare.
The blessed one, marveling at his faith, said, "Let the two of us stand in prayer, O friend."

And as the words of the prayer were being finished, while the sick man still lay prostrate, the Lord, who does the will of those who please him, heard the prayer of his servant too, and lightened the warfare for that brother.
And the two of them gave thanks to the Lord God.

Some people, driven by envy, called him a chatterer and an idle talker. He corrected them by deed, showing everyone in every way that he was capable of anything, since Christ gave him strength in all things. He kept silent for a whole year and said nothing at all to anyone, so that the envious themselves came to him as petitioners, saying:
"An ever-flowing spring has been shut off, and the salvation of all has perished."
After their entreaties he took up his former way again. Then everyone marveled at all his achievements, as if at some newly appeared Moses.
raised him to the headship of the brethren, a lamp upon the chief lampstand. And the good examiners, having pondered, were not mistaken.
But he too ascends the mountain, and passing through the impassable darkness, he receives the God-shaped lawgiving, led up by spiritual steps.
And having seen, he opens his mouth by the word of God, and he drew in the Spirit and belched forth a word and words, and the good treasures of the heart.

And he passed the end of his visible life instructing the Israelite monks. He differed from Moses in one thing only: the entry into the Jerusalem on high. In the case of the lower Jerusalem, Moses was in some way denied that entry.
And many bear witness who through these things were saved and are being saved. A good [?] witness is the new David, of the all-wise one's wisdom and salvation.
Our venerable pastor John is also a good witness. At his request, as a memorial, from Mount
To us this new God-seer, having come down from Sinai in thought [?],
showed us, he too, his tablets written by God: outwardly practical and inwardly contemplative.
which carry confirmation, and say this:
Glory be to our God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
